Listen to this article Share …Says quality of laws determines quality of governance Senate President Godswill Akpabio has urged political parties to reconsider decisions denying experienced lawmakers tickets to return to the National Assembly, warning that the practice could weaken legislative institutions and undermine democratic governance. Akpabio said legislative experience, competence and contributions to national development should be considered when parties select candidates for subsequent elections, arguing that the loss of experienced lawmakers deprives the legislature of valuable institutional knowledge. He spoke on Thursday while acknowledging the contributions of Professor Francis Faduyile, a former president of the Nigerian Medical Association (NMA), whom he said had considerable experience and expertise to contribute to the Senate. “It is not good for a senator to serve in the Senate for only one year and then leave. Political parties must take a closer look at their decisions, particularly when dealing with serious-minded individuals who can make meaningful contributions to legislation and national development,” Akpabio said. He added, “Denying such individuals tickets deprives the legislature of their experience.” The Senate President warned against treating the National Assembly as a platform for political patronage, insisting that legislative positions should be occupied by people capable of contributing to lawmaking and national development. “The Senate is not a place for sharing political largesse,” he declared. Read also: NEC endorses 90-day action plan to ease cost of living for Nigerians Akpabio acknowledged that political considerations within individual states often influence decisions on who gets party tickets. However, he urged political leaders to recognise the value of retaining lawmakers who have developed the experience needed to contribute meaningfully to legislative proceedings. Citing his experience in Akwa Ibom State, he said he had thanked the governor for supporting the return of three senators to the National Assembly. According to him, continuity in the legislature can improve the quality of debates, strengthen parliamentary institutions and support the development of laws capable of addressing Nigeria’s challenges. To illustrate the importance of legislative experience, Akpabio cited the United States, where some lawmakers have spent decades in the Senate. He referenced former United States Senator Robert Byrd, who represented West Virginia in the Senate for 51 years, and former President Joe Biden, who represented Delaware in the Senate from 1973 to 2009. “That is the kind of experience we are talking about,” Akpabio said. He argued that lawmakers who serve for extended periods acquire institutional knowledge and legislative expertise that can improve parliamentary proceedings and the quality of legislation. Akpabio said Nigeria needed to build a democratic system in which the legislature was recognised as a critical institution of governance rather than a platform for rewarding political loyalists. “We must ensure that the legislature is firmly entrenched in Nigeria’s democratic system and is not treated as a place for political compensation,” he said. He stressed that the quality of legislation passed by the National Assembly had implications for the effectiveness of government and the welfare of citizens. “It is a serious matter because the quality of our laws determines the quality of governance,” Akpabio said. “If we do not make good laws, how can we ensure that Nigeria is properly governed? We must enact laws that genuinely improve the lives of Nigerians,” he added. The Senate President urged lawmakers to remain committed to producing legislation that would strengthen democratic institutions, improve governance and deliver tangible benefits to citizens. He also referred to the recent Senate debate on the decriminalisation of suicide, which attracted considerable attention on social media, as an indication that Nigerians were following proceedings in the legislature. Akpabio welcomed the public interest generated by the debate, saying it should encourage senators to improve their contributions and ensure that legislative decisions reflected the public interest. He urged his colleagues to continue putting their best into their legislative responsibilities. “We must continue to put our best foot forward, deepen democracy through good laws and strengthen the legislature as a central institution of Nigerian democracy,” he said. Akpabio congratulated senators on their legislative work and urged them to proceed to their respective committees to continue deliberations on pending matters.
